newsitem.title: PAKISTAN: Pakistan shows dismal economic growth in 1996/97.
newsitem.headline: Pakistan shows dismal economic growth in 1996/97.

text.p: Pakistan's economy grew an estimated 3.1 percent in fiscal 1996/97 (July-June), a dismal effort compared with last year's 4.6 percent and a target of 6.3 percent, said a government survey released on Wednesday.
The growth rate was not far ahead of the population growth rate, which the Economic Survey 1996/97 put at 2.77 percent. Pakistan had 135.28 million people on January 1, it estimated.
"Value added in major crops and large-scale manufactures have suffered setbacks which have ultimately impacted the GDP (gross domestic product) growth," the survey said.
"It is one of the worst years in the last few years as far as economic indicators are concerned," Finance Minister Sartaj Aziz told a news conference.
"But within that, the most depressing figure is that of large-scale manufacturing, which for the first time in our history is minus 1.4 percent," he added.
The annual document, issued before Friday's budget for 1997/98, said agriculture expanded a nominal 0.7 percent against 1995/96 growth of 5.27 percent and a target of 5.0 percent.
Large-scale manufacturing shrank 1.4 percent, according to the survey, basing its estimates on the outcome of the first nine months of 1996/97.
It said the largely undocumented small-scale manufacturing sector grew 8.4 percent, reiterating an often-derided estimate that appears year after year.
Aziz said the 8.4 percent figure was derived by "a certain methodology" and might not reflect the actual growth in the small-scale sector and could be less than what the survey said.

Pakistan's major crops were struck by several vagaries of nature. Leaf curl virus and flies attacked cotton, severe frost and borers affected sugarcane, and prolonged drought followed by prolonged rains at harvest time hit wheat, the survey added.
It said the government had made a firm effort to control public expenditure and the budget deficit in 1996/97 despite a great decline in revenue.

The budget deficit will reach an estimated 6.2 percent of GDP compared to 6.3 percent in 1995/96, it said. Revenue collection reached only 221 billion rupees ($5.45 billion) in the first 10 months, against a whole-year target of 340 billion, it said, predicting an end-year shortfall of 50 billion rupees.
The survey said Pakistan had a labour force of 37.15 million with an estimated unemployment rate of 5.37 percent.
However, it defined employment very broadly to include any wage earner or self-employed person aged 10 or more who had worked at least one hour during an unspecified reference period.
It said annual consumer price inflation was likely to rise 11.62 percent in 1996/97, compared to 10.3 percent last year.
The survey said the balance of payments had come under pressure because exports had grown only 1.1 percent while imports grew 1.5 percent in July-April 1996/97.
